dek.text: Drones and ground robots triaged simulated casualties beside human medics at Disaster City in College Station. DARPA's director called the result not enough.

introduction.text: [TEEX staged the finals of DARPA's Triage Challenge at Disaster City in College Station from November 5th to November 13th](c1). [Disaster City is a {{number:c11}} acre mock community with full scale structures that can collapse, rubble piles and a derailed train](c11).

[Autonomous drones and ground robots worked alongside first responders there, triaging simulated mass casualty incidents and relaying critical data to human medics](c2). [The challenge seeks autonomous systems such as drones and robots that can assess injuries quickly, accurately and at scale](c8).

sections.heading: What the machines had to do

paragraphs.text: [Competitors had to show their systems could locate casualties, identify signs of injury and send critical data to medical response teams](c10). [Teams built technology to read vital signs from a distance and work alongside human medics](c18). [The program page says teams developed algorithms, aerial drones and ground vehicles meant to work with the medics who give hands on care](c9). Neither DARPA's account of the finals, its program page nor TEEX's account calls these systems artificial intelligence.

[The {{number:c14}} competitions included a simulated tornado ripping through a community market, smoke filled buildings, nighttime searches in near darkness and search and rescue under rubble](c14). [On the Human Machine Teaming night course a robot searched for casualties during a controlled explosion while role players took cover](c27). [That course simulated an attack on a forward operating base](c28), [and each team worked with assigned medics on it](c16).

[Moulage artists made hyper realistic mock injuries](c15), [and actors playing civilians moved through nearly a dozen timed preparation stations](c29). [DARPA's command post checked every mock casualty report against each patient's simulated injuries and vital signs](c13).

[More than {{number:c12}} participants from the military, universities, tech companies and startups competed for more than {{money:c12}} in cash prizes](c12). [RoboScout won the Systems competition and Disruptors won the Data competition](c3), at the prize amounts DARPA lists in its account of the finals. [A self funded two person team from Hawaii, called DRONE, placed second in the first trials](c24).

sections.heading: Why the director said it is not enough

paragraphs.text: [DARPA Director Stephen Winchell said human machine teams outperform every approach to the problem](c5). [He then said that result was not enough](c6). [He said some teams did well at identifying victims and others at triage, lifesaving or evacuation](c7). DARPA's account of the finals and TEEX's account give no lives saved, accuracy or rankings beyond the winners.

[DARPA has an open research topic, TRIAGE-X, for autonomous medical triage systems that recognize chemical toxidromes and physically deliver the antidote or a life saving intervention](c19). [It is open until November 25th, 2026](c20). Every casualty in the finals was simulated, and neither DARPA's account nor TEEX's describes any of these systems used in a real emergency.
